title: Understanding the Tom Lynch Salary: How to Convert Hourly Rates to Annual Pay and Estimate Tax & Super
description: Wondering about the Tom Lynch salary? Learn how to convert hourly rates to annual pay using the 38-hour week, plus tax brackets, Medicare levy, and superannuation.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, the annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives your gross annual pay before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and award rates?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage is the legal minimum for award-free employees, currently $26.44 per hour (from 1 July 2026). Award rates are set by the Fair Work Commission for specific industries and occupations, and are often higher. You can check your award using the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guides.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on an annual salary?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your salary at 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 (2026–27). For example, if your annual gross pay is $60,000, your employer must contribute an additional $7,200 into your super fund.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Hourly Rates to Annual Pay

If you're trying to make sense of a job offer or just want to compare your current wage, the conversion from hourly to annual is straightforward. The standard formula is:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For most full-time roles, we assume a 38-hour week, as this is the standard under the Fair Work system. For example, if you earn $30 per hour, your annual gross pay would be $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This is the figure before tax, Medicare, and super.

This method applies whether you're checking the **Tom Lynch salary** or your own pay. The same logic works for part-time or casual roles—just use your actual weekly hours.

## The National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

Australia has a safety net of minimum wages. From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, bringing their minimum to $33.05 per hour. This loading is paid on top of the base rate, not included in it.

Most employees are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that sets higher rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each award, listing minimum pay rates, allowances, and penalty rates. Always check your award before assuming the National Minimum Wage applies.

## Tax and the Medicare Levy

Once you have your annual gross figure, you can estimate your take-home pay using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- $0 – $18,200: Nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15c for each $1 over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: $4,020 plus 30c for each $1 over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: $31,020 plus 37c for each $1 over $135,000
- $190,001+: $51,370 plus 45c for each $1 over $190,000

In addition, the Medicare levy is generally 2% of your taxable income. For 2025–26, the single reduction threshold is used here (the 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed in this estimate). If your income is below a certain level, the levy may be reduced or waived.

For example, on an annual gross of $59,280, your tax would be approximately $4,020 + 30% × ($59,280 – $45,000) = $8,304, plus Medicare of $1,185.60, leaving an estimated take-home of about $49,790.40. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) guide for a more detailed breakdown.

## Superannuation Paid on Top

Employers must pay superannuation at 12% of your ordinary earnings, on top of your salary. This is not deducted from your gross pay. The super guarantee applies up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 (2026–27). For the $59,280 example, your employer would contribute an additional $7,113.60 into your super fund.

If you're self-employed or earning above the cap, different rules apply. See our [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) page for more.

## Fortnightly Pay and Cash Flow

Many employers pay fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross, multiply your weekly pay by 2. Using the $30/hour example: weekly gross = $30 × 38 = $1,140, so fortnightly = $2,280. After tax and Medicare, your fortnightly take-home would be roughly $1,915.

## Casual Loading and Other Considerations

If you're a casual employee, your hourly rate includes a 25% loading to compensate for lack of paid leave. When converting to annual, use the loaded rate. For example, a casual on the National Minimum Wage earns $33.05/hour, giving an annual gross of $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80. Our [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) page explains how this works.

Remember that the annual figure here assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. It's an estimate, not a determination of your actual pay.

## Using the Timesheet Tool

To quickly calculate your own figures, visit [the timesheet](/). Enter your base hourly rate and check the casual loading box if applicable. The tool will show your annual, fortnightly, and weekly amounts, along with estimated tax and super.

## Summary

Whether you're researching the **Tom Lynch salary** or planning your own budget, the conversion is simple: hourly × hours per week × 52. Use the 38-hour standard for full-time, adjust for part-time or casual, and always check your award for correct minimum rates. Then apply the tax brackets and Medicare levy to estimate take-home pay, and remember super is paid on top.
